title: Relationships and confounding

prerequisite.prompt: Can a survey of only one club establish the preference of all students?
prerequisite.answer: No; selection and coverage limit the claim.

vocabulary: Two variables vary together in observed data
A change in one factor produces a change in another
A factor related to both the proposed cause and outcome

blocks.text: In a fictional log, groups that practiced longer also scored higher: 1 hour with 4 points, 2 hours with 6 and 3 hours with 8. This pattern is an association. Prior experience could affect both practice choices and scores. The table alone cannot establish the effect of adding practice time.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
rows = [{"hours": 1, "score": 4},
        {"hours": 2, "score": 6},
        {"hours": 3, "score": 8}]
for row in rows:
    print(row["hours"], row["score"])

blocks.title: Follow the evidence
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right and connect the evidence to the stated rule.

blocks.text: The numbers rise together in these three invented records. A description such as higher practice hours went with higher scores is supported. A claim that one extra hour guarantees two more points goes beyond the observations. No statistical calculation is required to see this limit.

blocks.label: Name one factor besides practice duration that could influence both time chosen and score.

blocks.text: A chart title Practice causes success overstates the evidence. Replace it with Practice time and scores in three fictional records, and describe the possible confounder. Better wording does not repair the study, but it makes the report honest.

A fairer comparison could offer the same task, instructions and assessment and randomly assign fictional groups to practice conditions. In real classrooms, a teacher must approve any activity and protect equal learning opportunities; this lesson uses a paper plan.

blocks.label: Even a better comparison has only four fictional groups. What should be reported?

workbook.title: Describe the evidence
workbook.prompt: State the pattern in the three worked records without using caused or guaranteed.
workbook.answer: Higher recorded practice hours are associated with higher scores in these three records.

workbook.title: Identify a confounder
workbook.prompt: Explain how prior experience could relate to both practice time and score.
workbook.answer: Experienced learners may choose different practice amounts and also score higher even without additional practice.

workbook.title: Repair an overclaim
workbook.prompt: A learner predicts every student gains 2 points per extra hour. Explain why that is unsupported.
workbook.answer: The three observations do not establish a universal causal rule or predict every individual; other factors and variation are unmeasured.

workbook.title: Plan independently
workbook.prompt: A fictional dataset links more hints used with lower scores. Give a noncausal explanation and plan a fairer comparison of whether hints help.
workbook.answer: Learners finding tasks harder may use more hints and score lower. Use comparable tasks and starting skill, a teacher-approved or paper random-assignment plan, same outcome measure and report uncertainty; do not deny needed support.

workbook.title: State a remaining limit
workbook.prompt: Even a better comparison has only four fictional groups. What should be reported?
workbook.answer: Small size, constructed data, conditions and measured outcome; do not generalize broadly or claim classroom effectiveness.
